During the CrowdStrike outage, a user said a third-party application shouldn't be able to do this kind of damage to the OS. They argued Windows desktops and servers being blue-screened by an update may point to a Windows weakness as much as a CrowdStrike bug.

Recovery reports from affected users: "F8 + last known good configuration" worked for one team. Another said a Windows system restore helps, but isn't practical across an environment of ~500 or more clients.
Window resizing in Windows 11 is criticized as similar to macOS Tahoe: "You have to position the mouse just outside the window. It is non-intuitive and awful."
Comparison: one user said Linux these days provides a more refined and consistent UX than both macOS and Windows. Another said Windows 11 is "not exactly in a position to attract switchers."
One user regretted wiping Windows 10 from a laptop to install Ubuntu, saying "Windows 10 is not bad at all" and they'd have enjoyed keeping it for the new Ubuntu userland support (WSL).
"I've found the Windows 2012R2 to be my favorite OS for the desktop from the Windows family."
Workaround for the hidden local-account option in Windows setup: run setup without an internet connection, or type in a fake phone number a few times until it offers to create a local account.

A user who converted to an online Microsoft account found they couldn't set a password and were pushed to create a PIN. Without one, they had to log in with their complex Microsoft account password and needed their phone's password manager.

Long-standing bug: Windows names the local user folder with a truncated version of the online account name. The usual workaround (create an offline account first, then convert it) breaks if the offline option is removed.

A longtime Windows fan said Windows has become user-hostile, citing mandatory telemetry, forced updates, users treated as beta testers, and now pressure toward a Microsoft account. They are planning to switch to Linux.

A user who has paid for retail Windows 10 licenses complained that two consecutive updates broke Windows Search for people who disabled web results. Combined with forced cloud login, they're now looking at alternatives.

A family's Microsoft account was hacked and added as a child to a fake family, blocking software installs. Microsoft support couldn't remove it and suggested guessing the attacker's password. They wiped the PC and reinstalled with an offline account.
An industrial PC user stays on Windows 7 because Windows 10's forced updates and random restarts are unacceptable on 24/7 test rigs. They said stability was once why Windows won in this field.

Setting up a CI system, a user found Windows Server 2019 fast to set up, with a snappier UI, and it compiled the same C code in half the time of Windows 10. They called it the ultimate Windows apart from its pricing.
One user recommended Windows 10 LTSC as solving most Windows 10 problems.

Windows 11 widgets show celebrity gossip and sports trivia, which a user called absurd for an OS sold on productivity and costing $200. Another said there was no way to fully turn the articles off and switched to Pop!_OS.
A user who stayed on Windows only for gaming switched to Ubuntu MATE. Steam Proton ran their favorite games, battle.net, and the Diablo 4 beta perfectly, and Windows now runs only as a VM.
A user tried Linux but couldn't get their laptop working closed with a second screen, so they went back to Windows 10.
StartAllBack was recommended as a godsend for restoring the Windows 10-style taskbar on Windows 11.
"It gets easier and easier every year to want an alternative to Windows, but it remains impossible to actually switch, at least for me."
